result: P. falciparum has lost mitochondrial FASII enzymes but retains a divergent mitochondrial ACP (mACP) that lacks the conserved serine residue required for 4-phosphopantetheine (Ppant) modification, having replaced it with phenylalanine.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C20, C28, C36, and C37 are well-supported by BLAST analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing absence of mitochondrial FASII enzymes and sequence alignment data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) demonstrating the Ser-to-Phe substitution in mACP. The consistency between sequence analysis, prior citations, and phylogenetic data provides strong evidence for this structural divergence.

result: P. falciparum mACP localizes to the mitochondrion and undergoes post-translational processing upon import, with the mature protein beginning at or near Leu-51.
evaluation: Claims C32, C38, C39, C40, C41, C42, and C43 are supported by immunofluorescence colocalization with HSP60 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), Western blot analysis showing size differences between predicted (21 kDa) and observed (15 kDa) molecular mass (Figure 1C), and mass spectrometry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The co-migration of truncated Δ2-50 mACP with parasite-expressed mACP provides strong evidence for the processing site.

result: mACP is essential for P. falciparum blood-stage parasite viability, as demonstrated by ligand-dependent knockdown experiments showing parasite death in the third intraerythrocytic cycle upon mACP depletion.
evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C33, C44, C45, C46, and C47 are strongly supported by growth assay data (Figure 1E) showing normal growth for 3 days followed by major growth defect on day 4 in -aTc conditions, blood-smear analysis showing widespread parasite death (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), and Western blot confirmation of robust mACP knockdown (Figure 1E inset). The temporal pattern and reproducibility support essentiality.

result: P. falciparum lacks homologs of most LYR-motif proteins found in other eukaryotes but retains Isd11 (PF3D7_1311000), which shares 29% identity with human Isd11 and conserves the LYR sequence motif.
evaluation: Claims C52, C53, C54, C55, and C56 are supported by comprehensive BLAST analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with appropriate e-value cutoffs (3e-6 for Isd11, >0.01 for others) and sequence alignment data (Figure 2A) showing conservation of the LYR motif. The systematic search methodology and clear e-value thresholds provide confidence in the negative results for other LYR proteins.

result: P. falciparum mACP directly binds to Isd11 via the LYR motif and stabilizes the Isd11-Nfs1 complex required for Fe-S cluster biosynthesis.
evaluation: Claims C9, C34, C62, C64, C65, C68, C69, C70, and C71 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: mass spectrometry showing Nfs1 enrichment in mACP-HA2 IP samples (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), reciprocal co-IP experiments in parasites (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and E. coli (Figure 2F), LYR mutagenesis studies showing reduced/eliminated binding (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and purification of 1:1 mACP-Isd11 complex (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 6). The convergence of multiple experimental approaches provides robust support.

result: P. falciparum mACP binds Isd11 through a divergent molecular interface that does not require the Ppant group, with parasite Isd11 having replaced the conserved Arg-6 with isoleucine to accommodate the hydrophobic Phe113 of mACP.
evaluation: Claims C10, C35, C74, C75, C76, and C77 are supported by sequence analysis showing the Arg-to-Ile substitution in parasite Isd11 (Figure 2A), co-IP experiments demonstrating mACP-Isd11 interaction despite lack of Ppant (Figure 2D, 2F, 2G), and specificity experiments showing parasite Isd11 does not bind E. coli ACP or apicoplast ACP (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 7). The complementary sequence changes and binding specificity support co-evolution.

result: Structural modeling and mutagenesis studies demonstrate that Phe113 of mACP partitions into a hydrophobic pocket at the mACP-Isd11 interface and is critical for complex stability and parasite viability.
evaluation: Claims C82, C83, C84, C85, C86, C87, and C88 are supported by Rosetta structural modeling (Figure 3B), Ni-NTA pulldown experiments showing loss of co-purification with F113A mutant (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and growth assays demonstrating that F113A mACP cannot rescue parasites upon endogenous mACP knockdown (Figure 3D). The integration of computational and experimental validation provides strong support, though the structural model remains a prediction.

result: Knockdown of mACP causes loss of Nfs1 protein in P. falciparum parasites, indicating that Nfs1 stability is tightly coupled to mACP expression.
evaluation: Claims C11, C91, C92, C93, C94, and C95 are supported by Western blot analysis using a validated anti-Nfs1 antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing detection of ~60 kDa Nfs1 band in +aTc conditions but not in -aTc conditions (Figure 4A). The antibody validation in E. coli and appropriate molecular weight provide confidence, though densitometry analysis shows high variability (p=0.2) across replicates (Figure 4D).

result: Knockdown of mACP causes loss of the Rieske Fe-S protein in ETC complex III, while other mitochondrial proteins (HSP60, cyt c1) remain stable.
evaluation: Claims C12, C96, C97, and C98 are supported by Western blot analysis showing loss of epitope-tagged Rieske (~43 kDa) in -aTc conditions (Figure 4B) while HSP60 and cyt c1 levels are maintained (Figure 4B, 4C). The specificity of the effect strengthens the conclusion, though statistical analysis shows marginal significance for Rieske (p=0.07) (Figure 4D).

result: Decyl-ubiquinone (dQ) temporarily rescues parasites from death upon mACP knockdown for one intraerythrocytic cycle, indicating that ETC failure is the immediate cause of death but additional dysfunctions contribute to death on longer timescales.
evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C104, C105, C106, C107, C108, and C109 are supported by growth assay data (Figure 5A) showing dQ rescue in the third cycle but not beyond, compared to indefinite rescue from atovaquone. The temporal pattern of rescue provides strong evidence for ETC dysfunction as the immediate cause of death, with the limitation of rescue indicating additional essential functions. The comparison with atovaquone as a positive control strengthens the interpretation.

result: Proguanil treatment prevents dQ rescue and causes mitochondrial depolarization in mACP-depleted parasites, supporting the model that impaired ubiquinone recycling due to Rieske loss and ETC dysfunction is the immediate cause of parasite death.
evaluation: Claims C115, C116, and C117 are supported by growth assay data showing loss of dQ rescue with proguanil (Figure 5B) and microscopy analysis showing dispersed MitoTracker signal specifically in -aTc+proguanil conditions (Figure 5C, 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The statistical analysis (p=0.003) and mechanistic consistency with prior work on proguanil strengthen the conclusion.

result: The decoupling of mitochondrial Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity through retention of a Ppant-independent mACP is widespread among apicomplexan parasites (Toxoplasma, Babesia) and the chromerid Vitrella brassicaformis.
evaluation: Claims C13, C14, C134, C135, C136, and C137 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing divergent mACP homologs lacking the conserved Ser in multiple apicomplexan species and V. brassicaformis. The phylogenetic distribution and timing relative to loss of plastid photosynthesis provide evolutionary context, though functional validation in other species is lacking.

result: Background knowledge claims about eukaryotic mitochondrial FASII pathways, malaria epidemiology, P. falciparum mitochondrial metabolism, and apicoplast FASII.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C15, C16, C17, C18, C19, C21, C22, C23, C24, C25, C26, and C27 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior published work. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings.

result: Background knowledge claims about LYR proteins, mACP interactions in yeast and humans, and the Isd11-Nfs1 complex in other eukaryotes.
evaluation: Claims C29, C30, C31, C48, C49, C50, C51, C58, C59, C60, C61, C72, C73, C78, C79, C80, C81, C89, and C90 represent established knowledge from prior studies supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential comparative context for understanding the divergent features of the parasite system.

result: Background knowledge claims about the parasite ETC, ubiquinone recycling, mitochondrial membrane potential, and antimalarial drug targets.
evaluation: Claims C101, C102, C103, C111, C112, C113, C114, C118, C119, C120, and C121 represent established knowledge supported by citations to prior work. These provide necessary mechanistic context for interpreting the dQ rescue and proguanil experiments.

result: P. falciparum provides a new molecular paradigm for essential ACP function without an acyl-Ppant group, representing a parasite-specific adaptation that decouples Fe-S cluster biogenesis from FASII activity.
evaluation: Claims C122, C123, C124, C125, C126, C127, C128, C129, C130, C131, and C138 synthesize the major findings into a conceptual framework. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence (essentiality, Isd11 binding, Nfs1 stabilization, lack of Ppant) and comparison with other eukaryotes. The paradigm shift is justified by the data.

result: Loss of mACP destabilizes Nfs1, impairs Rieske stability and ETC complex III function, and leads to parasite death. P. falciparum lacks MZM1 homolog but retains cyt c1 upon mACP loss, suggesting accumulation of a late complex III assembly intermediate.
evaluation: Claims C139, C140, C141, C142, C143, C144, and C145 integrate multiple experimental observations (Western blots in Figure 4, growth assays in Figure 1E and Figure 5) with comparative analysis (BLAST for MZM1, comparison with yeast). The retention of cyt c1 levels (Figure 4C) supports the assembly intermediate model by analogy to yeast, though direct demonstration of the intermediate is lacking.

result: Respiratory failure is the immediate cause of parasite death upon mACP loss, but defects in other essential processes (potentially involving mitochondrial fumarate hydratase and/or cytoplasmic/nuclear Fe-S cluster proteins) contribute to death on longer timescales.
evaluation: Claims C146, C147, C148, and C149 are supported by the temporal pattern of dQ rescue (Figure 5A) showing rescue in cycle 3 but not beyond. However, C149 is speculative regarding the specific processes involved, as no direct evidence is provided for fumarate hydratase or cytoplasmic Fe-S cluster protein dysfunction. The inference is reasonable but requires further validation.

result: Background and speculative claims about cytoplasmic Fe-S cluster biogenesis, including the potential role of Mdr2 transporter and independence from mitochondrial Nfs1 in mammalian cells.
evaluation: Claims C150, C151, C152, and C153 are based on prior work in other organisms but lack direct experimental validation in P. falciparum. The dispensability of Mdr2 in blood-stage parasites (C152) and potential independence of cytoplasmic Fe-S cluster synthesis from mitochondrial Nfs1 (C153) create uncertainty about the mechanisms underlying the longer-term lethality of mACP loss.

result: P. falciparum mACP does not regulate mitochondrial translation, as evidenced by lack of L0R8F8 homolog, retention of cyt c1 levels upon mACP knockdown, and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential in -aTc conditions alone.
evaluation: Claims C154, C155, C156, C157, C158, C159, C160, and C161 are supported by BLAST analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), Western blot data showing stable cyt c1 (Figure 4C), and microscopy showing focal MitoTracker signal in -aTc conditions (Figure 5C). The convergence of multiple lines of negative evidence (absence of L0R8F8, retention of mitochondrial translation products and membrane potential) provides reasonable support for the conclusion.

result: Specificity controls for mACP interactions and effects of mACP knockdown, showing that mACP retains conserved Glu residues for LYR motif interaction, Isd11 was not detected in IP/MS samples, mACP does not interact with HSP60 or cyt c1, and HSP60/cyt c1 levels are maintained upon mACP knockdown.
evaluation: Claims C57, C63, C66, C67, C99, and C100 provide important specificity controls. The sequence conservation (C57) is well-documented (Figure 1A). The absence of Isd11 in IP/MS (C63) is explained by its small size. The negative controls for mACP interaction (C66, C67) and protein stability (C99, C100) are supported by co-IP and Western blot data (Figure 2E, Figure 4B, 4C), strengthening the specificity of the mACP-Isd11 interaction and effects on Nfs1/Rieske.

result: Speculative claims about additional functional/regulatory roles of ACP in Fe-S cluster biogenesis, comparison with anaerobic parasites lacking ACP/Isd11, and potential for additional mACP interactions in parasites beyond Isd11-Nfs1.
evaluation: Claims C132, C133, C162, and C163 are speculative and acknowledge uncertainty. C132 and C162 propose additional functions for mACP beyond those demonstrated, while C133 provides comparative context from other parasites. C163 notes that any additional interactions would diverge from known LYR-protein interactions. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work but lack direct experimental support.

result: Background claim that the mitochondrial ETC is essential for malaria parasite viability in all lifecycle stages.
evaluation: Claim C164 is supported by citation to prior published work and represents established knowledge providing context for the therapeutic relevance of the findings.
